In early September Joan pulled on her coat and hat and cane and set out for the parking lot. At seventy-four she still lovingly tended the garden every summer, and she had been anxious lately about getting it cleaned up before frost. Snow was possible tomorrow, and the new neighbors next door, a single man on disability, were not inclined to help, she had learned.

She drove slowly around the loop, hesitated at the gas pump, and saw a woman coming out of the 7-Eleven. Her vague face was familiar, and then Joan recognized that it was Manisha Scannell, who had bought the house next to hers the previous winter. She and Gary--and was that the Bauers, with little Emma?--had waded through piles of junk in the yard for three days that spring before making it fit for new owners. Manisha was an Indian woman from Boston, recently divorced; two little boys bouncing in her wake.

"Hold on," Joan said. "I need some advice."

Manisha stopped in her tracks. "Hi, did I see you at meetings last winter?" she asked, her smile paper-white and careful. "I met you so many times I think you were part of the new board, wasn't it?"

"Oh, right, help pick apples! I'll never forget the first fall meeting when the board president assigned chairs. Someone said, 'What does it matter whether we sit in that row or this row?' And you said, 'Look, we're all volunteers. You all deserve seats at the front.'"

JOAN WHITCOMB was the fictional centerpiece of a real panel discussion on civil liberties at the Annual Meeting of the American Small Town Professional Community in Rutland, Vermont, on June 2 in which Mark Moran took part. The scenario was a variation on a situation linked to the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which bans discrimination against people with disabilities and requires "reasonable accommodations" of them. In states that have adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, it's illegal to refuse to rent to people in wheelchairs unless the building was constructed before 1978 and, in the words of Vermont law, is "not readily adaptable to the needs of the disabled." But many Americans are opposed to ramps, lifts, and the other accommodations required by the act, and some judges and legislators have recently begun to question how far an individual's right goes when it comes, as it inevitably does, into conflict with the rights of others, including the desire of homeowners not to be burdened with expensive "special" requirements.

The Whitcomb hypothetical raised the question whether a homeowner's easement rights (the right to use the sidewalk in front of your house) can be nullified by a neighbor's need for a ramp. Does the neighbor have special rights because the disability is a natural condition (say, being born with spina bifida) rather than an accident; because the disability is permanent rather than temporary (like a broken leg); and because the person with the disability is the homeowner rather than a renter? What if a second neighbor with a disability moves in next door and wants a ramp, too? What if the person who needs the ramp is obese rather than a wheelchair user?

In their own debates over municipal tree permits, disability ramps, the obligation to provide child care, gun-control ordinances, and Ten Commandments displays, town officials across the country have found themselves in the middle of a new political and moral thicket. The language of rights and liberties is written large on the American political landscape, but it turns out that rights rub against one another all the time. The public conversation about rights tends to dwell on the dramatic clashes—the right to free speech versus the right to a fair trial, or the right to bear arms versus the right to be secure in one's home. He tucked his notes into his breast pocket and prepared to move on to the next item. Instead he was fixed by Joan's gaze. Her hands, which were knuckles and blue-veined, looked bigger to him all of a sudden.

"Mr. Pfeiffer," Joan said, "what about the spirit of mercy?"

He blinked. The club was silent.

"That ramp," she said, "saves my neighbors a lot of pain every time they come home. The rule you're enforcing makes my sale impossible and condemns me to sit, for the next however long I have, in a house I can't get out of. Are you really going to evict me by sticking to a rule no one intended to be a weapon?"

Someone coughed nervously.

Gary felt his cheeks get warm. "Ms. Whitcomb, that's not at all what we're—" A strange, high hopefulness seemed to fill the room.

"I'd like you to think about that," Joan said. "Just for a moment."

He closed his mouth. The others were watching him, too. It was as if the room had tilted. The air was thick; he was aware of his own pulse, of the even, shallow breathing of the couple beside him. They all looked at Joan and then back at Gary. No one spoke. It was like standing at the edge of a cliff and peering down, seeing nothing but air and then, when you step forward, feeling the certainty of solid ground.

Gary opened his mouth. "A ramp through the garage," he said, "which the homeowners association would allow, would comply with the city's guidelines and meet the letter and the spirit of our covenant."

He looked at the Bauers. They nodded.

Joan did not rise from her chair, but her mouth made the shape of a smile.

After the meeting, the mood in the clubhouse was subdued, and the hum of conversation stayed low as people filed out. Joan tried to hide a small smile, catching the satisfied look from her daughter in the corner. But the Bauers lingered, pale but determined.

The following week, Gary called a special working session. This time, he brought blueprints from his own attic – years of experience in his past life had made him a surprisingly practical problem-solver. He suggested a solution that respected both the homeowners’ covenants and Emma’s need for accessibility: a lightweight, folding aluminum ramp that could be stored indoors when not in use, paired with an unobtrusive side entrance for the Bauers' daughter.

It took discussion, negotiation, and even a few moments of awkward silence, but eventually everyone agreed. Terry Bauer, her hair a little less tidy than before but eyes clear, thanked Joan for pushing for a solution that could set a precedent for others. Joan softened. “What matters,” she said, “is that everyone feels safe and at home.”

In the end, the compromise restored a sense of harmony to Willow Creek. The ramp was discreet, yet functional, and the bylaws committee reviewed their regulations to be clearer about disabilities and reasonable accommodations. At the next meeting, Gary raised a toast with lemonade for all. No one minded the sweat on the glasses.

And Joan, who had always kept her cane close at hand, found herself reaching out to help carry in the welcome bundle of daffodils Terry brought as a thanks.

Rules, it seemed, could be guidelines for building community rather than walls that divided it. And as the summer sun poured through the clubhouse windows, everyone agreed that made a far better neighborhood than either side had imagined alone.

A lawnscape photographer once called the street her "most picturesque block." In early summer the fruit trees along the sidewalks, the clematis spilling over the hedges, the peppered maples swaying above the sidewalks, formed a green tunnel of abundance. The Bauers had sold their house in the next subdivision over and moved here because they loved the moody, rambling privet hedges and the old white fences, and their daughter had chosen the single-story house for the same reason. But in this neighborhood everyone had a different reason for loving the street: the ease of parking on the wide shoulder, the gentle grade down to the creek, the privacy, the darkness at night. And above all the beautiful landscaping, which came with rules.

The Bauers' ramp was twelve feet long, one-and-a-half inches high at its highest point, painted a pale, powder blue that matched their porch ceiling. It was the only spot of color and the only discordant note on the block. The couple walking their schnauzer paused to critique it from the sidewalk, calling it "medieval" and "brutalist." An elderly man driving by beeped his horn.

The story above is a slightly adapted version of an incident that happened in my hometown a few years ago, an incident which some of the people who were involved later discussed on the radio. (You can listen to that segment here). The incident generated a great deal of discussion and sympathy for everyone involved. But I think there were larger difficulties underlying the incident, ones that don't come up in the details of the story itself.

To see those larger issues, let's simplify the incident, abstracting it to something that can happen in all sorts of settings.

A neighborhood enacts a rule that says every house must meet a particular safety standard. The rule is justified by the need to keep everyone safe, and the builders of most new houses pitch in and comply, because they want their neighbors to be safe. But the cost of complying with the rule is higher for certain people than for others. And the people for whom the rule is more costly tend to be people who have already suffered some misfortune. Some of the neighbors complain, saying they don't want the "look" of these costlier alterations, and they urge the neighborhood association to enforce the rule more stringently. The association is sympathetic but also doesn't want to cause further anguish to the people who have already suffered a misfortune. So they're caught in a vise, and no matter how they rule, someone is going to be upset, and in fact everyone is going to be somewhat upset.

Because that's the problem. In situations like these you can't have it both ways. It isn't possible to have a rule that reliably improves overall safety and also doesn't impose additional costs on people who have already suffered some misfortune. That's why these situations are so wrenching. You can change the details—the nature of the rule, the kind of misfortune involved, which people are most likely to suffer the greater costs—but the core tradeoff never goes away.

Notwithstanding the headline on the story—the one that says "Wheelchair Ramp Sparks Fight" —this isn't a story about a fight. It's a story about a tradeoff that you can't win. And the shape of the tradeoff is clear if you consider the three parties involved:

Gary went on. "However...,"

Joan's heart leapt.

Gary said, "We're hearing a lot of emotion tonight and I understand it. But I'm not convinced this ramp is permanent. It may well come down next spring. And I think we all want to see Emma included." He paused. "I'm proposing...God, this is awkward," he said. "I'm proposing that we pass an emergency resolution to allow ramps in front yards during the following circumstances: when a resident provides a signed letter, from a licensed medical practitioner, that a ramp is essential for egress and ingress to the resident's home, and when the ramp is removed when the condition requiring the ramp no longer exists. This resolution would sunset at the end of our fiscal year. That gives us some time to revisit the bylaws. And it gives Emma what she needs for now.... That's my proposal."

Joan tried to rise, but her knees weren't cooperative.

Gary said, "If there's no objection...?"

Joan managed to wave her hand.

Gary nodded toward her. "Joan?"

She pulled herself up and addressed the group. "I think this is a good resolution, given the circumstances," she said. "I don't disagree with the Bauers' right to put in a ramp for their daughter. And I'm sure we'll all—if we're lucky—be in their shoes some day." She sat down.

The resolution passed, three to two.

As Joan packed her realtor's boxes, she pointed to the "No Front-Yard Structures" sign staked in the lawn next door. "See that?" she said to her daughter. "Promise me you'll take it down the day the ramp comes out."

She could see the Bauers' ramp, smooth and light-colored and bright as a vein. In a few months she would be somewhere else. But for now she waited for the light to change again and tried to imagine what this intersection might look like by winter. She imagined the snow coming down, white and silent and soft. She imagined the neighbors outside digging their cars out one more time while she watched from a window. She didn't answer. She unfolded her cane, stood up straight, and waited for him to put his hand on her shoulder so she could lean on him as they crossed the tile floor to the door.

Two years earlier her husband of twenty-five years had died of a heart attack in his sleep, and by the time her kidneys failed she needed dialysis three times a week. That was where she met Gary, in the waiting room of the clinics on the other side of town, and he was one of the few who did not flinch when she said her hands smelled like urine. Joan sat in her car for a long time after the meeting. Then she phoned her daughter and said, "It didn't work out. We'll stay here for now." After that, she drove to the house where Gary Pfeiffer lived and knocked on his door, something she had never done.

Gary sighed. "I understand your concern, Joan. But we're not talking about a basketball court. We're talking about a young woman trying to live with some semblance of dignity."

"But what about the property values?" Joan asked. "What about the aesthetics?"

Gary turned to the board members. "We can amend the bylaws later if we need to," he said. "But right now, we should prioritize people. We should prioritize doing what's right."

Joan stood up, her cane clattering on the floor. “This is not right!” she said, and walked out, shaking her head.

The next day, two other neighbors came to Joan, saying they were thinking of challenging the decision. They suggested a petition. Joan agreed to help, but her heart wasn't in it. She had always been proud of Willow Creek, of its order and its standards. But now, looking at the ramp, she felt a sense of loss. It wasn't just about her house. It was about a world she no longer recognized.

Then she remembered something. Three years ago, the town had been debating whether to put in sidewalks. She had spoken against it, saying it would ruin the character of the neighborhood. Old Man Hemmings, who’d used a walker after his hip replacement, had spoken in favor. She remembered thinking he was making a big deal out of nothing.

She sat down at her kitchen table and stared out the window. She thought about Emma Bauer, trying to get into her house. She thought about herself, struggling with the stairs. Maybe, she thought, doing what's right wasn't about preserving the past. Maybe it was about making room for the future, even if it didn't look quite like she expected. She picked up the phone and called her daughter. "How's the apartment looking?" she asked. "I think it might be time to look again."

**Analysis:**

This story is a compelling portrait of community conflict and the complexities of rules, fairness, and empathy. Here's an analysis of key elements:

*   **The Central Conflict:** The conflict isn't *simply* about a ramp or flowers. It's about perceived preferential treatment and Joan's feeling of being undervalued as a long-time resident.  Her desire for a fair application of the rules stems from a deeper emotional need to feel respected within the community.  The story cleverly layers the ramp and flower issues to show a pattern.
*   **Gary Pfeiffer's Complexity:** Gary is not portrayed as a villain. He seems reasonable and thoughtful. His justification for allowing the ramp – prioritizing a human need over strict rule adherence – sounds noble. *However*, his subsequent action of targeting Joan’s tire swing flowers undercuts that goodwill and reveals a pattern of behavior suggesting he is making a point. It is likely he wanted to demonstrate that the accommodation for the Bauers was not simply bending the rules and that rules would continue to be applied to everyone, even long-term residents.
*   **Joan's Perspective:** The story does a good job of making the reader sympathize with Joan. Her vulnerability (bad knees, needing to sell her house) makes her predicament more poignant. Her anger is justified, especially when she sees the contradiction in the HOA’s actions. Willow Creek is three square miles of dry expanse north of Tucson, laid out from scratch thirty years ago, before the monsoon season.

Until now the neighborhood has been separated, by gated entrances and willow-lined common roads, from the bustle of the main city. There's not so much as a rectory or daycare nearby, let alone a nursing home. Nothing between Willow Creek and the hospital but two-fat freeway ramp as wide as a baseball field.

Everyone knows everyone. Most families share a house, car, sports team, child, pet, or birth date with at least one other. A clique of nannies sits in the playground pavilion when it gets hot enough to fry eggs outside. Men gather on the teepy for weekend baseball, sometimes afternoons with wives and kids on Sundays. And the kids from all the schools go swimming and hide and seek in the park without supervision.

"Secluded, peaceful, and livable" is the neighborhood's selling point. Bake Sale: Cheap, Effective Threats

Gary and his crew folder over 2,000 flyers and hand them out at Farmer's and Dewar. They set up tables on main street and make donuts and frosted cupcakes and sugar cookies. Gary spends a hundred bucks on lavender-scented baggies.

After exactly one day the baking stops. The Bauers have given up. The ramp will be in the garage. Rather than pay the price for hardening their position, they backed down and settled. There is no mention of the bake sale.

This isn't the way people normally test the strength of their threats. Usually we harden up our threats to find out just how obstinate we really are. We don't build flexibility into them; we don't threaten to make a half-baked compromise. Doing so would contradict our very purpose: to make the other side's costs more severe. But Gary's policy is different that way. It allows him to be firm before getting to a yes. His threat reveals a deeper willingness to be reasonable. The Bauers move past Gary's formal no, to the yes he articulates in the form of a threat. Baking a cake is too precious and costly for some of the things we allow people to make our lives miserable.
